title: Naskh
def: Abrogation: the replacing of one ruling by a later one, as God wills.
what: The Quran says that whatever verse God abrogates or causes to be forgotten, He brings one better or similar (2:106). Muslims point to clear cases: the prayer direction changed from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:142–150), and the prohibition of wine came in stages (4:43, then 5:90–91).

The term is mainly about rulings of law. Later scholars cut the number of cases drastically: al-Suyuti kept about twenty, and Shah Waliullah five. Some, such as Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, denied abrogation within the Quran altogether.
misread: That Muhammad cancelled the peaceful verses with violent ones, so Islam is violent.
sources: Some early exegetes made sweeping claims that one verse cancelled many. Many scholars rejected this, and the principles the Quran repeats are not treated as cancelled: no compulsion in religion (2:256), kindness and justice to those who have not fought you over your religion (60:8), and the command to deal fairly even with those one dislikes (5:8).
